terms.grammar: with an indirect question in the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Att. 16.5.2: incrēdibile est quam mē in omnī genere dēlectārit
Cic. Att. 13.23.3: incrēdibile est quam ego ista nōn cūrem
Cic. Att. 5.15.1: sed est incrēdibile quam mē negōtī taedeat
Sen. Ep. 49.1: incrēdibile est quam recēns dēsīderium tuī fēcerint
terms.comment: How Cicero’s letters say it: the news follows in the question. Latin puts it as a statement, not as a forecast of what the hearer will believe.

terms.grammar: with an indirect question in the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Att. 13.26.2: crēdibile nōn est quantum scrībam
Cic. Att. 2.23.2: crēdibile nōn est quantum ego in cōnsiliīs prūdentiā tuā … pōnam

terms.gloss: that’s unbelievable, you don’t say (the hearer’s reply)

phrases.latin: Incrēdibile est quam multa jam verba puer nōverit.
phrases.english: You won’t believe how many words the boy knows already.

phrases.latin: sed quam diū fuit, incrēdibile est quam mē in omnī genere dēlectārit
phrases.english: but as long as he was here, you wouldn’t believe how he delighted me in every way

phrases.latin: equidem crēdibile nōn est quantum scrībam, quīn etiam noctibus; nihil enim somnī.
phrases.english: You wouldn’t believe how much I’m writing, even at night: I get no sleep.

phrases.latin: Sine dōte ille illam in tantās dīvitiās dabit? nōn crēdibile dīcis. — At tū edepol nūllus crēduās.
phrases.english: He’ll give her into such wealth without a dowry? You can’t be serious. — Well then, don’t believe it.

sources: Lewis & Short: incredibilis · Lewis & Short: credibilis
